column2: On a wide screen, harbor does the same job, but the edges are different.
A rail down the side, a notch at the side, a hinge in the middle, and on a television, a safe band all the way round.
A bar can claim any edge. On a tablet, the navigation rail is a solid bar at the start.
The page sits beside it, and its rows keep their margin from the rail.
Start and end follow reading order. In a right-to-left language, the rail moves to the right.
Turn a phone on its side, and the system edges move to the sides, around the notch.
The list still runs edge to edge, while its rows keep clear of it.
A dual-screen phone has a hinge down the middle.
Sheets, dialogs and toasts keep to one screen, never across it.
On a television, the system edges are the title-safe band around the edge of the screen.
A scaled screen lays the page out on a reference screen, and scales it to fit.
Every edge claimed once, whatever the screen.
